title: Cisco lets 27-year-old rewrite legacy code with unlimited AI tokens
excerpt: Cisco gave Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy unlimited AI tokens to refactor 98% of its legacy code in 24 months.
body:
Why a 27-year-old got the biggest refactor at Cisco  

Cisco’s president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel walked into a San Francisco round-table, pointed at Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, “Paddy” to his colleagues, and said, “You have unlimited AI tokens, go nuts.” The 27-year-old ex-founder of the real-time translation startup EzDubs, which Cisco bought in 2025, was suddenly tasked with rewriting roughly 98 % of the company’s legacy codebase.

Patel found Paddy “buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic,” five levels below him, and gave him a four-week sprint to prove that a two-person team could modernize the monolith. If the sprint succeeds, the plan calls for a 24-month effort to refactor the bulk of Cisco’s code. The source for this story is Fortune’s report [link](https://fortune.com/2026/10/30/cisco-president-jeetu-patel-gen-z-27-year-old-unlimited-ai-tokens-rewrite-legacy-code-entry-level-jobs/).

The reader will learn how unlimited AI tokens reshape a refactor, why Patel deliberately creates tension between junior and senior staff, and what concrete steps other teams can take if they want to try a similar approach.  

## Unlimited AI tokens turn a cautious edit cycle into rapid prototyping  

Patel’s “unlimited tokens” are usage credits for generative-AI models that can write, test, and suggest code changes. With no cost ceiling, Paddy can fire off thousands of prompts each day, ask the model to map call graphs across the monolith, suggest modular boundaries, and generate unit tests for newly created components.

The AI also scans for deprecated APIs and security-critical patterns that have accumulated over decades. Because the token limit is gone, the workflow shifts from a slow, incremental edit loop to a rapid-prototype mindset.

The trade-off is volume. An unchecked flood of AI-generated patches can overwhelm reviewers. Patel’s “go nuts” permission assumes a disciplined gate: code owners still approve changes, and automated testing catches regressions. The financial barrier disappears, but the engineering discipline barrier remains.  

A short example shows the difference. A traditional refactor might require a developer to write a helper script to list all calls to a legacy library:

```python
import ast, os

def find_calls(root, lib):
    calls = []
    for dirpath, _, files in os.walk(root):
        for f in files:
            if f.endswith('.py'):
                tree = ast.parse(open(os.path.join(dirpath, f)).read())
                for node in ast.walk(tree):
                    if isinstance(node, ast.Call) and getattr(node.func, 'id', '') == lib:
                        calls.append((f, node.lineno))
    return calls
```

With unlimited tokens, the same developer can prompt the model:

```
"List every place in the repo where the function `legacy_api` is called and suggest a replacement with `new_api`."
```

The model returns a ready-to-apply patch and a set of unit tests, cutting hours of manual work.  

## Intentional tension between junior and senior staff  

Patel believes “tension is good.” He places a Gen Z engineer next to veterans to force idea-level friction. Senior staff bring deep system knowledge and an understanding of legacy constraints; a junior newcomer asks questions that seasoned engineers may never consider.  

The source notes that Patel worries “if you don’t hire early-in-career workers, where do fresh ideas get injected?” He also admits that mixing generations can create personality clashes, but he tries to “create enough friction on the ideas” while avoiding personal conflict. Trust, according to Patel, is the foundation for setting “unreasonable goals.”  

In practice, the tension shows up during code reviews. A senior engineer might push back on an AI-generated suggestion that appears to break an existing contract. Paddy can point to the model’s reasoning and performance data, forcing the senior to validate the legacy impact. The dialogue surfaces hidden dependencies and validates both the AI’s output and the organization’s constraints.  

## A concrete timeline for the 24-month refactor  

Patel gave Paddy four weeks to prove the concept. The sprint includes three milestones:  

1. Discovery (Weeks 1-2), AI maps the entire codebase, identifies high-risk modules, and produces a dependency graph.  
2. Pilot refactor (Week 3), A small, self-contained service is rewritten using AI-generated code and unit tests.  
3. Review and scale (Week 4), Senior architects evaluate the pilot, set quality gates, and define the rollout plan for the next 24 months.  

If the pilot meets the quality gates, the team expands to larger subsystems, always pairing AI output with senior oversight. The source does not provide exact dates for the rollout, but the 24-month horizon is the stated final goal.  

## Risks and mitigations  

Output overload is a real risk: unlimited tokens can produce more patches than reviewers can handle. The mitigation is to enforce a daily limit on pull requests and require automated static analysis before human review.

Model hallucination, suggesting code that compiles but behaves incorrectly, calls for end-to-end integration tests for each AI-generated module. Cultural pushback from senior staff can be eased by framing the effort as a partnership, not a replacement, and highlighting that senior engineers still own final approval.

## The takeaway  

Unlimited AI tokens let a junior engineer iterate at a scale senior staff could not afford, while deliberate tension with veterans ensures that each iteration is vetted by deep institutional knowledge. Teams that want to replicate this model should give capable early-career talent unrestricted AI resources, pair them with senior mentors, and manage the inevitable idea-level friction with clear quality gates and trust-building practices.
